generation.hypothesis: Tuning the elemental ratios in FeCoNiTi-type high-entropy alloys to induce a sharp, first-order magnetic transition at room temperature will enhance the magnetocaloric effect, producing higher magnetic entropy change (ΔS) and adiabatic temperature change (ΔT) under moderate magnetic fields.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic or near-equiatomic FeCoNiTi high-entropy alloy exhibiting multiple ferromagnetic transitions without a dominant first-order transition.
generation.intervention: Optimize the composition by adjusting the ratios of Fe, Co, Ni, and Ti to promote a sharp, first-order magnetic phase transition near room temperature.
generation.conditions: Near room temperature operation under moderate magnetic fields (approximately 1–3 Tesla).
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of a distinct first-order magnetic phase transition, likely through controlled phase separation (e.g., tuning the fcc and C14 phase balance).
generation.mechanism: A first-order magnetic phase transition generally results in abrupt changes in magnetization, leading to a substantial magnetic entropy change and a pronounced adiabatic temperature shift. Fine-tuning the elemental ratios in the alloy is hypothesized to trigger such a transition, thereby improving the magnetocaloric performance while utilizing cost-effective, abundant elements.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tailored FeCoNiTi alloy will show enhanced magnetocaloric properties with a larger ΔS and ΔT under moderate magnetic fields compared to the baseline equiatomic composition.
generation.baseline: Standard equiatomic (or near-equiatomic) FeCoNiTi high-entropy alloy without compositional optimization, which exhibits multiple ferromagnetic transitions but lacks a sharply defined first-order transition.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvement is expected under moderate magnetic fields (1–3 Tesla) and room temperature conditions; deviations in processing or the presence of undesired secondary phases may limit the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimized composition and processing conditions required to achieve the targeted first-order transition are not precisely known, and slight variations may affect the magnitude of the observed magnetocaloric effects.

Perform controlled thermal treatments to ensure phase homogeneity. Measure the magnetization and magnetic entropy change (ΔS) as well as the adiabatic temperature change (ΔT) under moderate applied magnetic fields (1-3 T) over a temperature range near room temperature.
measurements: Magnetization vs. temperature and field curves
Direct or indirect measurements of adiabatic temperature change (ΔT)
Structural characterization (XRD, SEM/TEM) to verify phase structure and detect the presence of a first-order transition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the compositional variations result in a distinct first-order magnetic phase transition near room temperature and no significant enhancement in ΔS and ΔT is observed compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

frame.goal: Identify and design a material that exhibits enhanced magnetocaloric properties, such as a larger entropy change (ΔS) and adiabatic temperature change (ΔT) under practical magnetic field strengths.
frame.limitation: Existing materials often require very high magnetic fields, are expensive (e.g., rare-earth based), or do not perform efficiently near room temperature, limiting their practical application in cooling systems.

decision.trend: Earlier studies in high‐entropy and multi‐component alloys have focused on tuning magnetic properties via compositional substitutions and thermal treatments. For example, PMC6197204 demonstrated that substituting Co with Cr and adjusting annealing temperatures can modulate phase decomposition and magnetic parameters in AlCoFeNi‐based alloys, while later work in PMC11375712 revealed that an equiatomic FeCoNiTi alloy exhibits multiple ferromagnetic transitions with notably high coercivity in its fcc phase. These investigations highlight how composition-driven changes can be exploited to manipulate magnetic ordering and transitions, although they did not specifically target the magnetocaloric effect.
decision.unsolved: While significant progress has been made in tuning magnetic transitions and reducing reliance on rare‐earth elements, there remains a gap in deliberately engineering alloys to achieve a large entropy change and adiabatic temperature shift under moderate magnetic fields near room temperature. The challenge is to combine cost‐effective, abundant elements with a composition that triggers a first-order magnetic transition optimized for magnetocaloric performance.
decision.lever: Optimize the elemental ratios (e.g., fine-tune the Fe, Co, Ni, and Ti content in FeCoNiTi-type high-entropy alloys) to induce a first-order magnetic phase transition exactly at room temperature, thereby maximizing the magnetic entropy change (ΔS) and adiabatic temperature change (ΔT) under moderate fields.
decision.why: This step builds on the trend of using compositional adjustments to modulate magnetic transitions, as seen in previous work. Given that FeCoNiTi alloys show multiple ferromagnetic transitions and high coercivity, tuning their composition is a natural next step to target a sharp, first-order transition that can yield an enhanced magnetocaloric effect while keeping material costs low and performance suitable under moderate fields.
